title: The same query, 4,000 times slower since last night
intro: The order-history page took 5 ms yesterday and takes 20 seconds today. No deploy, no schema change, no traffic spike. The only event overnight was a data import: 30 million historical rows were bulk-loaded into order_items from an acquired company. The query joins orders to order_items for one customer.

steps.prompt: Look at the plan with real numbers. Run EXPLAIN ANALYZE on: SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id WHERE o.customer_id = 8812
expected_commands: psql -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id WHERE o.customer_id = 8812;"
psql -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id WHERE o.customer_id = 8812"
psql -c "EXPLAIN (ANALYZE) SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id WHERE o.customer_id = 8812;"
psql -c "EXPLAIN (ANALYZE, BUFFERS) SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id WHERE o.customer_id = 8812;"

   Hash Cond: (i.order_id = o.id)
   ->  Seq Scan on order_items i  (cost=0.00..271000.00 rows=14410021 width=96) (actual time=0.02..15220.30 rows=44410021 loops=1)
   ->  Hash  (cost=411.00..411.00 rows=88 width=84) (actual time=0.41..0.41 rows=88 loops=1)

steps.prompt: It reads all of order_items sequentially, and the planner thinks the table has 14.4 million rows (rows=14410021) when it really has 44.4 million. The planner's idea of a table comes from statistics. Check when order_items was last analyzed: select relname, n_live_tup, n_mod_since_analyze, last_analyze, and last_autoanalyze from pg_stat_user_tables where relname = 'order_items'.

Run the same EXPLAIN ANALYZE again to confirm the plan changed.
expected_commands: psql -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id WHERE o.customer_id = 8812;"
psql -c "EXPLAIN ANALYZE SELECT * FROM orders o JOIN order_items i ON i.order_id = o.id WHERE o.customer_id = 8812"

Nested Loop  (cost=0.99..1204.40 rows=210 width=180) (actual time=0.05..4.10 rows=212 loops=1)
   ->  Index Scan using idx_orders_customer_created on orders o  (rows=88) (actual rows=88)
   ->  Index Scan using idx_order_items_order_id on order_items i  (rows=2) (actual rows=2 loops=88)
 Execution Time: 4.31 ms
steps.hint: The same command as the first step.

resolution: The query didn't change and neither did the indexes. What changed was the planner's picture of the data. PostgreSQL chooses a plan by estimating how many rows each step will produce, using statistics that ANALYZE collects by sampling each table. The overnight import tripled order_items, but the statistics still described the old table, so the planner costed its options against a table that no longer existed and picked a hash join over a full scan of 44 million rows. With fresh statistics it chose 88 index lookups instead, and the query went from 20 seconds to 4 ms. Autoanalyze would have fixed this by itself eventually; it was queued behind three large vacuum jobs, because the default of three workers is shared by every table in the cluster. The signature to remember is in the plan: an estimated row count (rows=) far from the actual one. Whenever those differ by a large factor, suspect statistics before you suspect the query. Prevention: make ANALYZE the last step of every bulk load, restore, or major-version upgrade (pg_upgrade carries no statistics over in older versions, which produces this exact incident across a whole database); raise autovacuum_max_workers on clusters with many large tables; and for columns whose values are skewed or correlated, raise the statistics target or create extended statistics so the estimates are better to begin with.
real_commands_used: psql EXPLAIN ANALYZE (compare estimated and actual rows)
